# site is versioned with mike (see .github/workflows/docs.yml).

site_description: Trend estimation for long-term ecological survey data, in Python.
site_author: Computational Ecology Lab, University of Example
site_url: !ENV [READTHEDOCS_CANONICAL_URL, "https://survtrend.readthedocs.io/en/latest/"]
repo_url: https://github.com/ecolab-uni/survtrend
repo_name: ecolab-uni/survtrend
edit_uri: edit/main/python/docs/
copyright: Copyright © 2021–2026 Amelia Martin, Jun Chen and contributors

theme:
  name: material
  custom_dir: docs/overrides
  logo: assets/logo.svg
  favicon: assets/favicon.png
  icon:
    repo: fontawesome/brands/github
  palette:
    - media: "(prefers-color-scheme: light)"
      scheme: default
      primary: teal
      accent: amber
      toggle:
        icon: material/weather-night
        name: Switch to dark mode
    - media: "(prefers-color-scheme: dark)"
      scheme: slate
      primary: teal
      accent: amber
      toggle:
        icon: material/weather-sunny
        name: Switch to light mode
  features:
    - content.code.annotate
    - content.code.copy
    - content.tabs.link
    - navigation.footer
    - navigation.indexes
    - navigation.sections
    - navigation.tabs
    - navigation.top
    - search.highlight
    - search.suggest
    - toc.follow

watch:
  - src/survtrend

plugins:
  - search
  - autorefs
  - gen-files:
      scripts:
        - docs/scripts/gen_ref_pages.py
  - literate-nav:
      nav_file: SUMMARY.md
  - section-index
  - mkdocstrings:
      default_handler: python
      handlers:
        python:
          paths: [src]
          inventories:
            - https://docs.python.org/3/objects.inv
            - https://numpy.org/doc/stable/objects.inv
            - https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/objects.inv
            - https://docs.xarray.dev/en/stable/objects.inv
            - https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/objects.inv
          options:
            docstring_style: numpy
            docstring_section_style: table
            docstring_options:
              ignore_init_summary: true
            filters: ["!^_", "^__init__$"]
            heading_level: 2
            members_order: source
            merge_init_into_class: true
            separate_signature: true
            show_root_heading: true
            show_signature_annotations: true
            show_source: false
            show_symbol_type_heading: true
            signature_crossrefs: true
  - mkdocs-jupyter:
      # Notebooks are executed in CI only; locally the stored outputs are used.
      execute: !ENV [MKDOCS_EXECUTE_NOTEBOOKS, false]
      include_source: true
      ignore: ["notebooks/scratch/*.ipynb"]
  - bibtex:
      bib_file: docs/references.bib
      csl_file: docs/assets/ecology.csl
  - git-revision-date-localized:
      enable_creation_date: true
      fallback_to_build_date: true

markdown_extensions:
  - abbr
  - admonition
  - attr_list
  - def_list
  - footnotes
  - md_in_html
  - tables
  - toc:
      permalink: true

  - pymdownx.arithmatex:

  - pymdownx.details
  - pymdownx.emoji:

  - pymdownx.inlinehilite
  - pymdownx.snippets:

openapi: 3.1.0
info:
  title: Ecolab Survey Data API
  version: 1.4.0
  summary: Read-only access to the lab's long-term insect monitoring data.
  description: |
    The Survey Data API serves the harmonised Malaise-trap and light-trap data
    collected by the Computational Ecology Lab since 2004.

    * All endpoints are **read-only**; data entry happens in the field app.
    * Dates use ISO 8601 (`YYYY-MM-DD`) and coordinates are WGS 84 (EPSG:4326).
    * For large downloads, use the asynchronous `/exports` endpoints instead of paging through `/observations`.

    Data are licensed under [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Please cite the data paper ([doi:10.5281/zenodo.1234567](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.1234567)) when you use them in a publication.
  contact:
    name: Ecolab data team
    email: data@ecolab.example.edu
    url: https://ecolab.example.edu/data
  license:
    name: CC BY 4.0
    identifier: CC-BY-4.0
servers:
  - url: https://api.ecolab.example.edu/v1
    description: Production
  - url: http://localhost:8000/v1
    description: Local development stack (docker compose)
tags:
  - name: sites
    description: Monitoring sites and their habitat covariates.
  - name: observations
    description: Individual trap catches.
  - name: exports
    description: Asynchronous bulk downloads as CSV or Parquet.
security:
  - apiKey: []

paths:
  /sites:
    get:
      tags: [sites]
      operationId: listSites
      summary: List monitoring sites
      parameters:
        - $ref: "#/components/parameters/Limit"
        - $ref: "#/components/parameters/Cursor"
        - name: habitat
          in: query
          description: Only return sites of this habitat type.
          schema:
            $ref: "#/components/schemas/Habitat"
        - name: bbox
          in: query
          description: Bounding box as `min_lon,min_lat,max_lon,max_lat`.
          schema:
            type: string
            pattern: '^-?\d+(\.\d+)?(,-?\d+(\.\d+)?){3}$'
          example: "11.9,51.2,12.6,51.5"
      responses:
        "200":
          description: A page of sites.
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: "#/components/schemas/SitePage"
        "401":
          $ref: "#/components/responses/Unauthorized"

  /observations:
    get:
      tags: [observations]
      operationId: listObservations
      summary: List trap catches
      description: |
        Returns catches ordered by `date_emptied` and then by `trap_id`.
        Biomass is the wet weight after draining, in milligrams; see the
        [field protocol](https://ecolab.example.edu/protocols/malaise-v3.pdf)
        for details.
      parameters:
        - $ref: "#/components/parameters/Limit"
        - $ref: "#/components/parameters/Cursor"
        - name: site_id
          in: query
          description: One or more site IDs, comma-separated.
          schema:
            type: array
            items: {type: string, pattern: "^[A-Z]{2}-\\d{2}$"}
          style: form
          explode: false
          example: [GR-01, GR-17]
        - name: from
          in: query
          schema: {type: string, format: date}
          example: "2015-04-01"
        - name: to
          in: query
          schema: {type: string, format: date}
      responses:
        "200":
          description: A page of observations.
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: object
                required: [items, next_cursor]
                properties:
                  items:
                    type: array
                    items:
                      $ref: "#/components/schemas/Observation"
                  next_cursor:
                    type: [string, "null"]
        "400":
          $ref: "#/components/responses/BadRequest"
        "401":
          $ref: "#/components/responses/Unauthorized"

  /exports:
    post:
      tags: [exports]
      operationId: createExport
      summary: Request a bulk export
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              type: object
              required: [format]
              properties:
                format: {type: string, enum: [csv, parquet]}
                site_ids: {type: array, items: {type: string}}
                years: {type: array, items: {type: integer, minimum: 2004}}
      responses:
        "202":
          description: Export accepted; poll `/exports/{export_id}` until `status` is `ready`.
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: "#/components/schemas/Export"

  /exports/{export_id}:
    get:
      tags: [exports]
      operationId: getExport
      summary: Check the status of an export
      parameters:
        - name: export_id
          in: path
          required: true
          schema: {type: string, format: uuid}
      responses:
        "200":
          description: Export status, with a download link once it is ready.
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: "#/components/schemas/Export"
        "404":
          $ref: "#/components/responses/NotFound"

components:
  securitySchemes:
    apiKey:
      type: apiKey
      in: header
      name: X-API-Key
      description: Request a key from data@ecolab.example.edu. Keys are personal and must not be shared.
  parameters:
    Limit:
      name: limit
      in: query
      schema: {type: integer, minimum: 1, maximum: 1000, default: 100}
    Cursor:
      name: cursor
      in: query
      description: Opaque cursor returned as `next_cursor` by the previous page.
      schema: {type: string}
  schemas:
    Habitat:
      type: string
      enum: [dry_grassland, wet_meadow, pasture, forest_edge, arable_margin]
    Site:
      type: object
      required: [site_id, name, habitat, location]
      properties:
        site_id: {type: string, example: GR-17}
        name: {type: string, example: Hohe Wiese (Nord)}
        habitat: {$ref: "#/components/schemas/Habitat"}
        location:
          type: object
          description: Trap position (WGS 84). Coordinates of sensitive sites are rounded to 0.01°.
          properties:
            lon: {type: number, minimum: -180, maximum: 180}
            lat: {type: number, minimum: -90, maximum: 90}
        last_year: {type: [integer, "null"], description: "`null` while the site is still active."}
    SitePage:
      type: object
      required: [items, next_cursor]
      properties:
        items: {type: array, items: {$ref: "#/components/schemas/Site"}}

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Seasonal anomalies and long-term trends in Malaise-trap biomass.

Reads the harmonised trap catches exported from the field database,
aggregates them to monthly site-level biomass and estimates a log-linear
trend for every site, with moving-block bootstrap confidence intervals.

Usage: python python_script.py data/raw/catches.csv --out results/ --n-boot 999
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import logging
from datetime import date
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import xarray as xr

logger = logging.getLogger("biomass_trends")

REQUIRED_COLUMNS = ("site_id", "trap_id", "date_set", "date_emptied", "biomass_mg")

# fmt: markdown
METHODS_NOTE = r"""
## Trend model

For each site $s$ we regress the log-scale monthly biomass anomaly on time,

$$
\log B_{s,t} - \overline{\log B}_{s,m(t)} = \alpha_s + \beta_s \, t + \varepsilon_{s,t},
$$

where $m(t)$ is the calendar month of observation $t$ and $\overline{\log B}_{s,m}$ is the site-specific climatology for month $m$. The slope $\beta_s$ is reported as a *percentage change per decade*, $100 \times (e^{10 \beta_s} - 1)$.

Confidence intervals come from a moving-block bootstrap with blocks of 12 months, which preserves the within-year autocorrelation of the residuals [@kunsch1989].
"""

# fmt: markdown
DATASET_CARD = """
# Malaise-trap biomass trends

Generated by `python_script.py` on {created}.

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Sites | {n_sites} |
| Months | {n_months} |
| Bootstrap replicates | {n_boot} |

Files in this folder:

- `biomass_monthly.nc` – monthly biomass per site (mg per trap-day) and the seasonal anomalies
- `trends.csv` – one row per site with the slope, its bootstrap interval and the number of months used
- `METHODS.md` – a short description of the trend model

Please cite the data paper (doi:10.5281/zenodo.1234567) if you reuse these files.
"""


def load_catches(path: Path, *, min_trap_days: int = 7) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Read raw Malaise-trap catches and drop incomplete sampling intervals.

    Parameters
    ----------
    path : pathlib.Path
        CSV export from the field database, one row per trap emptying.
    min_trap_days : int, default 7
        Minimum number of days a trap must have been running for its catch
        to be kept.

    Returns
    -------
    pandas.DataFrame
        Catches with parsed dates and two extra columns, ``trap_days`` and
        ``biomass_per_day`` (mg per trap-day).

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If any of the required columns is missing from the export.
    """
    catches = pd.read_csv(path, parse_dates=["date_set", "date_emptied"], dayfirst=True)
    missing = set(REQUIRED_COLUMNS) - set(catches.columns)
    if missing:
        raise ValueError(f"{path} is missing required columns: {', '.join(sorted(missing))}")

    catches["trap_days"] = (catches["date_emptied"] - catches["date_set"]).dt.days
    short = catches["trap_days"] < min_trap_days
    logger.info("Dropping %d of %d catches with fewer than %d trap-days", short.sum(), len(catches), min_trap_days)
    catches = catches.loc[~short].copy()
    catches["biomass_per_day"] = catches["biomass_mg"] / catches["trap_days"]
    return catches


# fmt: markdown
# ### Why monthly aggregation?
#
# Trap emptying intervals vary between *7 and 21 days* depending on the season and on staff availability, so raw catches are not comparable across sites or years. We therefore
#
# 1. convert each catch to a daily rate (mg per trap-day),
# 2. spread that rate over every day the trap was running, and
# 3. average the daily rates within each calendar month.
#
# Months with fewer than `min_days` trap-days are set to **missing** rather than
# imputed, as agreed at the 2023 data meeting (see issue #142).
def to_monthly(catches: pd.DataFrame, *, min_days: int = 10) -> xr.DataArray:
    """Aggregate catches to monthly mean biomass per trap-day.

    Parameters
    ----------
    catches : pandas.DataFrame
        Output of :func:`load_catches`.
    min_days : int, default 10
        Months with fewer trap-days than this are set to NaN.

    Returns
    -------
    xarray.DataArray
        Monthly biomass with dimensions ``(site, time)``, where ``time`` is
        the first day of each month.
    """
    days = [pd.date_range(s, e, inclusive="left") for s, e in zip(catches["date_set"], catches["date_emptied"])]
    daily = (
        catches.assign(day=days)
        .explode("day")
        .astype({"day": "datetime64[ns]"})
        .groupby(["site_id", "day"])["biomass_per_day"]
        .mean()
        .reset_index("site_id")
    )
    monthly = daily.groupby("site_id")["biomass_per_day"].resample("MS").agg(["mean", "count"])
    monthly.loc[monthly["count"] < min_days, "mean"] = np.nan

    biomass = monthly["mean"].to_xarray().rename({"site_id": "site", "day": "time"})
    biomass.name = "biomass"
    biomass.attrs.update(units="mg trap-day-1", long_name="Monthly mean Malaise-trap biomass")
    return biomass


def seasonal_anomaly(biomass: xr.DataArray) -> xr.DataArray:
    """Log-scale anomaly relative to each site's monthly climatology.

    Parameters
    ----------
    biomass : xarray.DataArray
        Monthly biomass with dimensions ``(site, time)``.

    Returns
    -------
    xarray.DataArray
        ``log(biomass)`` minus the site-specific mean of ``log(biomass)`` in
        the same calendar month. Zero catches are replaced by half the
        smallest positive value at that site before taking logs.
    """
    floor = biomass.where(biomass > 0).min("time") / 2
    log_b = np.log(biomass.where((biomass > 0) | biomass.isnull(), floor))
    climatology = log_b.groupby("time.month").mean("time")
    anomaly = log_b.groupby("time.month") - climatology
    return anomaly.drop_vars("month").rename("anomaly")


def block_bootstrap_slope(
    y: np.ndarray, *, n_boot: int = 999, block: int = 12, rng: np.random.Generator | None = None
) -> tuple[float, float, float]:
    """Least-squares slope with a moving-block bootstrap interval.

    Parameters
    ----------
    y : numpy.ndarray
        One-dimensional series of monthly anomalies; NaNs are ignored.
    n_boot : int, default 999
        Number of bootstrap replicates.
    block : int, default 12
        Block length in months.
    rng : numpy.random.Generator, optional
        Random number generator, for reproducibility.

    Returns
    -------
    slope : float
        Slope in units of ``y`` per year.
    lower, upper : float
        Bounds of the 95 % percentile interval. All three values are NaN if
        fewer than three blocks of data are available.
    """
    rng = np.random.default_rng() if rng is None else rng
    t = np.arange(y.size) / 12.0
    ok = ~np.isnan(y)
    if ok.sum() < 3 * block:
        return np.nan, np.nan, np.nan
    slope, intercept = np.polyfit(t[ok], y[ok], deg=1)
    resid = y - (intercept + slope * t)

    n_blocks = int(np.ceil(y.size / block))
    starts = rng.integers(0, y.size - block + 1, size=(n_boot, n_blocks))
    idx = (starts[..., None] + np.arange(block)).reshape(n_boot, -1)[:, : y.size]
    boot = intercept + slope * t + resid[idx]
    keep = ~np.isnan(boot)
    slopes = np.array([np.polyfit(t[k], b[k], deg=1)[0] for b, k in zip(boot, keep)])
    lower, upper = np.percentile(slopes, [2.5, 97.5])
    return float(slope), float(lower), float(upper)


def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> None:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__.splitlines()[0])
    parser.add_argument("catches", type=Path, help="CSV export of trap catches")
    parser.add_argument("--out", type=Path, default=Path("results"), help="output directory")
    parser.add_argument("--n-boot", type=int, default=999, help="number of bootstrap replicates")
    parser.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=20240311)
    args = parser.parse_args(argv)

    logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(message)s")
    rng = np.random.default_rng(args.seed)
    args.out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    biomass = to_monthly(load_catches(args.catches))
    anomaly = seasonal_anomaly(biomass)

    rows = []
    for site in anomaly["site"].values:
        y = anomaly.sel(site=site).values
        slope, lower, upper = block_bootstrap_slope(y, n_boot=args.n_boot, rng=rng)
        rows.append({"site_id": site, "slope": slope, "lower": lower, "upper": upper, "n_months": int((~np.isnan(y)).sum())})
    trends = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    for col in ["slope", "lower", "upper"]:
        trends[f"{col}_pct_decade"] = 100 * (np.exp(10 * trends[col]) - 1)

    xr.Dataset({"biomass": biomass, "anomaly": anomaly}).to_netcdf(args.out / "biomass_monthly.nc")
    trends.to_csv(args.out / "trends.csv", index=False, float_format="%.4f")
    (args.out / "METHODS.md").write_text(METHODS_NOTE.lstrip(), encoding="utf-8")
    card = DATASET_CARD.format(
        created=date.today().isoformat(), n_sites=len(trends), n_months=biomass.sizes["time"], n_boot=args.n_boot
    )
    (args.out / "README.md").write_text(card.lstrip(), encoding="utf-8")
    logger.info("Median trend: %.1f %% per decade", trends["slope_pct_decade"].median())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

We reanalyse 20 years (2004–2023) of standardised Malaise-trap catches from 42 protected grassland sites with generalised additive mixed models that account for sampling effort, weather and site turnover.

## Introduction

Insects make up the majority of described animal species and provide services such as pollination, pest control and nutrient cycling on which both natural and agricultural systems depend [@losey2006; @noriega2018]. Over the past decade, a series of studies has reported marked declines in insect abundance, biomass and diversity, most prominently a 76 % loss of flying-insect biomass in German nature reserves over 27 years [@hallmann2017]. These findings received wide public attention, but they also raised methodological questions about site turnover, changes in sampling effort and the extrapolation from a limited set of locations to whole landscapes [@didham2020; @daskalova2021].

Here we revisit the question with a dataset that was designed for trend estimation from the outset: the same 42 sites were sampled every year with identical traps, and the effort was recorded for every emptying. We ask three questions:

1. How much has flying-insect biomass changed between 2004 and 2023, after accounting for sampling effort?
2. Do the trends differ between grassland types?
3. To what extent are the trends explained by weather during the sampling season?

## Methods {#sec-methods}

### Study sites and sampling

Malaise traps of the Townes type were operated at 42 sites from April to October each year (@tbl-sites). Traps were emptied every 7 to 21 days, and the catches were stored in 80 % ethanol and weighed after a standardised draining procedure[^draining]. In total, the dataset comprises 18,204 trap emptyings and 1.2 million trap-days.

[^draining]: Samples were drained through a 0.5 mm sieve for exactly 60 seconds and weighed to the nearest 0.01 g, following the protocol of @ssymank2018.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-sites
#| tbl-cap: "Monitoring sites, trap-years and median sampling interval by grassland type."
import pandas as pd

sites = pd.read_csv("data/sites.csv")
(
    sites.groupby("grassland_type")
    .agg(
        sites=("site_id", "nunique"),
        trap_years=("trap_year", "size"),
        median_interval=("interval_days", "median"),
    )
    .reset_index()
    .rename(columns=lambda c: c.replace("_", " ").capitalize())
    .style.hide(axis="index")
    .format(precision=0)
)
```

### Statistical model

We modelled the biomass $y_{ij}$ of catch $j$ at site $i$ with a Tweedie generalised additive mixed model with log link [@wood2017]:

$$
\log \mathbb{E}(y_{ij}) = \log d_{ij} + \beta_0 + f_1(t_{ij}) + f_2(\mathrm{doy}_{ij}) + \mathbf{x}_{ij}^\top \boldsymbol{\gamma} + u_i,
\qquad u_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_u^2),
$$ {#eq-gam}

where $d_{ij}$ is the number of trap-days, $f_1$ is a thin-plate regression spline of time, $f_2$ is a cyclic cubic spline of day of year, and $\mathbf{x}_{ij}$ contains the weather covariates (mean temperature, precipitation sum and mean wind speed during the trapping interval). Site-specific deviations from the overall trend were included as a factor-smooth interaction. We summarise the trend in @eq-gam as the percentage change in predicted biomass between 2004 and 2023.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why a Tweedie distribution?

Biomass is a continuous, non-negative quantity with exact zeros: traps that were emptied after a cold, rainy week are sometimes empty. The Tweedie family with power parameter $1 < p < 2$ handles both features without adding an arbitrary constant before a log transformation.
:::

Models were fitted in R with `mgcv::bam()`; this document only post-processes the saved predictions in Python.^[The model-fitting script is `analysis/fit_models.R` in the repository.]

## Results

Across all sites, biomass declined by 31 % between 2004 and 2023 (@fig-trend). The decline was steepest in wet meadows and weakest in dry grasslands (@tbl-trends), and it was remarkably consistent across sites: 37 of the 42 site-specific trends were negative.

```{python}
#| label: fig-trend
#| fig-cap: "Predicted biomass per trap-day by grassland type, from the model in @eq-gam with the weather covariates held at their means. Shaded bands are 95 % confidence intervals."
#| fig-alt: "Line chart with three declining lines, one per grassland type, falling from about 9 to about 6 grams per trap-day between 2004 and 2023."
#| echo: true
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

colours = {"Dry grassland": "#2a78d6", "Wet meadow": "#eb6834", "Pasture": "#1baf7a"}
pred = pd.read_csv("results/predictions.csv")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5))
for gtype, df in pred.groupby("grassland_type"):
    ax.fill_between(df["year"], df["lower"], df["upper"], color=colours[gtype], alpha=0.15, linewidth=0)
    ax.plot(df["year"], df["fit"], color=colours[gtype], linewidth=2, label=gtype)
ax.set(xlabel="Year", ylabel="Biomass (g per trap-day)", ylim=(0, None))
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper right")
plt.show()
```

| Grassland type | Sites | Change 2004–2023 | 95 % CI |
|:---------------|------:|-----------------:|:-----------|
| Dry grassland | 14 | −18 % | −29 to −6 % |
| Wet meadow | 11 | −44 % | −55 to −31 % |
| Pasture | 17 | −29 % | −38 to −19 % |
| **All sites** | **42** | **−31 %** | **−39 to −22 %** |

: Estimated change in biomass between 2004 and 2023 by grassland type, from the model in @eq-gam. {#tbl-trends}

Weather explained much of the year-to-year variation but little of the long-term trend. Adding the weather covariates reduced the residual deviance by 23 % but changed the estimated overall decline only from −33 % to −31 %.

::: {.callout-warning title="Interpreting the 2020 season"}
Sampling in 2020 started six weeks late because of pandemic restrictions. The cyclic smooth of day of year accounts for the missing spring catches, but the 2020 estimate has a wider confidence interval than other years and should not be over-interpreted.
:::

## Discussion

Our results confirm that flying-insect biomass in protected grasslands has declined substantially over the last two decades, although the decline is less steep than the 76 % reported by @hallmann2017 for a longer period. Because our design held sites, traps and protocols constant, the estimate is unlikely to be an artefact of site turnover, which has been suggested as an explanation for some earlier results [@didham2020]. The stronger decline in wet meadows is consistent with the drying of these habitats during the exceptionally dry summers of 2018, 2019 and 2022, an effect that our season-level weather covariates may not capture fully.

Several limitations should be kept in mind. Biomass is a coarse measure that can mask changes in community composition: a decline in large-bodied species may be offset by an increase in small ones, or vice versa. Malaise traps also sample a specific part of the flying-insect community, dominated by Diptera and Hymenoptera, and say little about ground-dwelling or nocturnal taxa. Finally, although all sites are protected, most are small and surrounded by intensively managed farmland, so the trends we observe may reflect pressures acting at the landscape scale rather than within the reserves themselves (see @sec-methods for the site selection criteria).

## Data and code availability {.unnumbered}

The data are available from Zenodo [@martin2026data] and the analysis code from <https://github.com/ecolab-uni/insect-biomass-2026>. The analysis can be reproduced with `quarto render` after creating the conda environment described in `environment.yml`.

# Long-term trends in Malaise-trap biomass
#
# Fits a negative-binomial GLMM (lme4) and, optionally, a Bayesian version of
# the same model (brms) to site-year biomass totals, and draws the figures for
# the 2026 monitoring report.
#
# Author:  Amelia Martin <a.martin@ecolab.example.edu>
# Created: 2024-03-11
# =============================================================================

# Setup ----

library(tidyverse)
library(lme4)
library(broom.mixed)
library(here)

run_brms <- FALSE # the Bayesian model takes about 40 minutes on the lab server
reference_year <- 2012
habitat_colours <- c(dry_grassland = "#2a78d6", wet_meadow = "#eb6834", pasture = "#1baf7a")
habitat_labels <- c(dry_grassland = "Dry grassland", wet_meadow = "Wet meadow", pasture = "Pasture")

set.seed(20240311)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 11))

# fmt: markdown
# ## Analysis plan
#
# 1. Read the harmonised catches and the site covariates from `data/derived/`.
# 2. Aggregate the catches to **site-year** totals and keep the number of trap-days as the effort variable; site-years with fewer than 60 trap-days are dropped.
# 3. Fit the frequentist model with `glmer.nb()` and check convergence with
#    `allFit()`.
# 4. If `run_brms` is `TRUE`, refit the model in brms with weakly informative priors and compare the posterior trend with the lme4 estimate.
#
# *Note:* site `GR-17` was moved by 300 m in 2015. Following the protocol, it is treated as a single site throughout.

# Helpers ----

#' Convert calendar years to decades since a reference year
#'
#' @param year A numeric vector of calendar years.
#' @param ref The reference year, which becomes zero.
#'
#' @return A numeric vector of decades since `ref`.
#' @examples
#' year_to_decade(c(2004, 2012, 2023))
year_to_decade <- function(year, ref = reference_year) {
  (year - ref) / 10
}

#' Percentage change from a slope on the log scale
#'
#' @param beta A numeric vector of slopes on the log scale.
#'
#' @return The corresponding percentage change, `100 * (exp(beta) - 1)`.
pct_change <- function(beta) {
  100 * (exp(beta) - 1)
}

#' Read a derived CSV file, failing early if it does not exist
#'
#' @param file Path to the file, relative to the project root.
#' @param ... Further arguments passed on to [readr::read_csv()].
#'
#' @return A tibble.
read_derived <- function(file, ...) {
  path <- here(file)
  if (!file.exists(path)) {
    stop("Cannot find ", path, ". Run `targets::tar_make()` first.", call. = FALSE)
  }
  read_csv(path, show_col_types = FALSE, ...)
}

# Data ----

catches <- read_derived("data/derived/catches_harmonised.csv")
sites <- read_derived("data/derived/sites.csv", col_types = cols(site_id = col_character()))

site_years <- catches |>
  mutate(year = lubridate::year(date_emptied)) |>
  group_by(site_id, year) |>
  summarise(
    biomass_mg = sum(biomass_mg, na.rm = TRUE),
    trap_days = sum(trap_days),
    n_emptyings = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(trap_days >= 60) |>
  left_join(sites, by = "site_id") |>
  mutate(
    decade = year_to_decade(year),
    grassland_type = factor(grassland_type, levels = names(habitat_labels)),
    site_id = factor(site_id)
  )

count(site_years, grassland_type)

# Model ----

fit_nb <- glmer.nb(
  round(biomass_mg) ~ decade * grassland_type + scale(spring_temp) + (1 + decade | site_id),
  offset = log(trap_days),
  data = site_years,
  control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa", optCtrl = list(maxfun = 2e5))
)

# All optimizers should agree to within a few percent; if not, say so in the report.
fit_all <- allFit(fit_nb)
summary(fit_all)$fixef

trend_table <- tidy(fit_nb, effects = "fixed", conf.int = TRUE) |>
  filter(str_detect(term, "decade")) |>
  mutate(across(c(estimate, conf.low, conf.high), pct_change))

# fmt: markdown
model_notes <- "
## Model notes

The primary model is a *negative-binomial* GLMM with a random intercept and a random slope for each site:

- the response is the total biomass (mg, rounded to integers) per site-year,
- `log(trap_days)` enters as an offset, so effects are on the scale of biomass per trap-day,
- year is centred on 2012 and expressed in decades.

Convergence warnings from `glmer.nb()` were checked with `allFit()`; all optimizers gave trend estimates within 2 % of each other.
"

writeLines(model_notes, here("output", "model_notes.md"))

if (run_brms) {
  library(brms)

  priors <- c(
    prior(normal(0, 1), class = "b"),
    prior(exponential(1), class = "sd"),
    prior(lkj(2), class = "cor")
  )

  fit_brm <- brm(
    round(biomass_mg) ~ decade * grassland_type + scale(spring_temp) +
      (1 + decade | site_id) + offset(log(trap_days)),
    data = site_years,
    family = negbinomial(),
    prior = priors,
    chains = 4, iter = 4000, warmup = 1000, cores = 4,
    backend = "cmdstanr",
    file = here("models", "brm_biomass_nb"),
    seed = 20240311
  )

  pp_check(fit_brm, ndraws = 100)
}

# Figures ----

pred <- expand_grid(
  decade = seq(min(site_years$decade), max(site_years$decade), length.out = 50),
  grassland_type = factor(names(habitat_labels), levels = names(habitat_labels)),
  spring_temp = mean(site_years$spring_temp),
  trap_days = 1
)
pred$fit <- predict(fit_nb, newdata = pred, re.form = NA, type = "response")

p_trend <- ggplot(site_years, aes(decade * 10 + reference_year, biomass_mg / trap_days)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = site_id), colour = "grey75", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line(data = pred, aes(y = fit, colour = grassland_type), linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = habitat_colours, guide = "none") +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_number(suffix = " mg")) +
  facet_wrap(vars(grassland_type), labeller = labeller(grassland_type = habitat_labels)) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Biomass per trap-day (log scale)",
    title = "Malaise-trap biomass, 2004–2023",
    caption = "Grey lines: individual sites. Coloured lines: population-level trend from the negative-binomial GLMM."
  )

# Site-level slopes: the reference habitat uses `decade` directly, the others
# add their interaction term.
site_slopes <- coef(fit_nb)$site_id |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "site_id") |>
  left_join(distinct(site_years, site_id = as.character(site_id), grassland_type), by = "site_id") |>
  mutate(
    slope = decade + case_match(
      grassland_type,
      "wet_meadow" ~ `decade:grassland_typewet_meadow`,
      "pasture" ~ `decade:grassland_typepasture`,
      .default = 0
    ),
    pct_decade = pct_change(slope),
    site_id = fct_reorder(site_id, pct_decade)
  )

p_slopes <- ggplot(site_slopes, aes(pct_decade, site_id, colour = grassland_type)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey60", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = habitat_colours, labels = habitat_labels) +
  labs(x = "Change per decade (%)", y = NULL, colour = "Grassland type") +
  theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())

ggsave(here("figures", "biomass_trend.pdf"), p_trend, width = 18, height = 9, units = "cm")
ggsave(here("figures", "site_slopes.pdf"), p_slopes, width = 12, height = 16, units = "cm")

input.content: # survtrend [![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/ecolab-uni/survtrend/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/ecolab-uni/survtrend/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml) [![CRAN status](https://www.r-pkg.org/badges/version/survtrend)](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=survtrend) [![Codecov test coverage](https://codecov.io/gh/ecolab-uni/survtrend/graph/badge.svg)](https://app.codecov.io/gh/ecolab-uni/survtrend) [![Lifecycle: stable](https://img.shields.io/badge/lifecycle-stable-brightgreen.svg)](https://lifecycle.r-lib.org/articles/stages.html#stable) [![DOI](https://zenodo.org/badge/DOI/10.5281/zenodo.1234567.svg)](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.1234567) survtrend estimates population trends from long-term ecological survey data, such as butterfly transects, Malaise traps or breeding-bird counts. It wraps generalised linear and additive mixed models in a consistent interface that takes care of the details that make monitoring data awkward: uneven sampling effort, missing years, observer effects, and sites that join or leave the scheme. The package is developed at the Computational Ecology Lab, University of Example, and is used to produce the annual reports of several regional monitoring programmes. ## Installation Install the released version from [CRAN](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=survtrend) with: ``` r install.packages("survtrend") ``` Or install the development version from [GitHub](https://github.com/ecolab-uni/survtrend): ``` r # install.packages("pak") pak::pak("ecolab-uni/survtrend/r") ``` A Python implementation with the same modelling core is available from PyPI and conda-forge: ``` bash pip install survtrend # or mamba install -c conda-forge survtrend ``` ## Usage ``` r library(survtrend) data(grassland_moths) grassland_moths #> # A tibble: 3,412 × 6 #> site_id year visit count effort habitat #> #> 1 GR-01 2004 1 37 6.5 dry_grassland #> 2 GR-01 2004 2 52 7 dry_grassland #> 3 GR-01 2004 3 41 6 dry_grassland #> # ℹ 3,409 more rows ``` Fit a trend model with an offset for sampling effort and a random intercept for each site: ``` r fit <- fit_trend( count ~ s(year) + habitat, data = grassland_moths, family = "nbinom2", effort = effort ) fit #> negative binomial (nbinom2), log link #> 42 sites, 20 years (2004–2023), 3,412 visits #> #> Overall change 2004–2023: -27.4% (95% CI -35.1% to -18.9%) ``` `tidy()`, `glance()` and `autoplot()` methods make it easy to use the results with the rest of the tidyverse: ``` r tidy(fit, exponentiate = TRUE) autoplot(fit, type = "partial", terms = "s(year)") ``` See `vignette("survtrend")` for a complete walk-through and `vignette("model-families")` for advice on choosing between Poisson, negative-binomial and zero-inflated models. ## Main functions | Function | Purpose | |----------|---------| | `read_survey()` | Read and validate exports of the field app | | `check_design()` | Summarise visits per site and year, and flag gaps | | `fit_trend()` | Fit a trend model with effort offsets and site effects | | `compare_trends()` | Pairwise differences between site-level trends | | `simulate_counts()` | Simulate survey data for power analyses | ## Citation If you use survtrend in a publication, please cite both the methods paper and the version of the software you used: ``` r citation("survtrend") ``` ``` bibtex @article{martin2024survtrend, title = {survtrend: Flexible trend estimation for long-term ecological monitoring data}, author = {Martin, Amelia and Chen, Jun and Okafor, Ngozi and M{\"u}ller, Lena}, journal = {Methods in Ecology and Evolution}, year = {2024}, volume = {15}, number = {7}, pages = {1203--1215}, doi = {10.1111/2041-210X.14321} } @software{survtrend_software, author = {Martin, Amelia and Chen, Jun and others}, title = {survtrend: Trend Estimation for Long-Term Survey Data}, version = {1.3.0}, year = {2026}, publisher = {Zenodo}, doi = {10.5281/zenodo.1234567} } ``` ## Related work - [rtrim](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=rtrim) implements the TRIM model used by Statistics Netherlands and many European bird and butterfly monitoring schemes. - [poptrend](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=poptrend) fits smooth population trends with GAMs and bootstrapped confidence intervals. - [mgcv](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=mgcv) and [glmmTMB](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=glmmTMB) provide the model-fitting engines used under the hood. - [unmarked](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=unmarked) and [spOccupancy](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=spOccupancy) model imperfect detection, which survtrend deliberately ignores; use them when detection probability is likely to change over time. - The [Living Planet Index](https://www.livingplanetindex.org/) methodology aggregates population trends across many species and regions. ## Code of Conduct Please note that the survtrend project is released with a [Contributor Code of Conduct](https://ecolab-uni.github.io/survtrend/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.html). By contributing to this project, you agree to abide by its terms.

--- title: "Supplementary Material S2: Detection probability of nocturnal moths at light traps" author: - Ngozi Okafor - Jun Chen - Amelia Martin date: "`r format(Sys.Date(), '%d %B %Y')`" output: bookdown::html_document2: toc: true toc_float: true number_sections: true code_folding: hide bookdown::word_document2: reference_docx: templates/supplement.docx bibliography: references.bib csl: methods-in-ecology-and-evolution.csl link-citations: true editor_options: markdown: wrap: sentence chunk_output_type: console --- ```{r setup, include=FALSE} knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4) library(tidyverse) library(unmarked) moths <- readRDS(here::here("data", "derived", "moth_counts.rds")) moths_wide <- readRDS(here::here("data", "derived", "moth_counts_wide.rds")) obs_covs <- readRDS(here::here("data", "derived", "moth_obs_covs.rds")) n_sites <- n_distinct(moths$site_id) n_nights <- n_distinct(moths$night_id) ``` # Overview This supplement describes how we estimated the detection probability of nocturnal moths at automated light traps. It complements the main text, where we report abundance trends corrected for imperfect detection. All analyses were run in R `r getRversion()` with the packages listed in Appendix \@ref(software). Light traps attract moths from an unknown, weather-dependent area, so raw counts confound changes in abundance with changes in detectability. We therefore used a repeated-count design: on each of `r n_nights` trap nights at `r n_sites` sites, the catch was recorded at 23:00, 01:00 and 04:00 CEST. Under the closure assumption, the three counts are replicate samples of the same local population, which allows abundance and detection to be separated with an N-mixture model [@royle2004; @kery2016]. # Data ## Sampling protocol Traps were run only on nights with a forecast minimum temperature above 8 °C and wind speeds below 4 Bft. Each trap consisted of a 15 W actinic tube above a funnel and a collecting box filled with egg trays. Moths were identified to species in the field where possible (e.g. *Noctua pronuba*, *Agrotis exclamationis*); difficult taxa, i.e. most *Eupithecia* and the *Oligia* complex, were retained for genitalia dissection. Nights with technical failures (power cuts, broken tubes, flooded boxes) were excluded before the analysis. Table \@ref(tab:effort) summarises the sampling effort by year. Effort was lower in 2020 because of travel restrictions. It returned to the planned 24 nights per site from 2021 onwards. Did this gap bias the trend estimates? We address this question in Section \@ref(sensitivity). ```{r effort} moths |> distinct(year, site_id, night_id) |> group_by(year) |> summarise(nights = n(), sites = n_distinct(site_id)) |> mutate(nights_per_site = round(nights / sites, 1)) |> knitr::kable( col.names = c("Year", "Trap nights", "Sites", "Nights per site"), caption = "Sampling effort by year.", booktabs = TRUE ) ``` # Model ## N-mixture model For site $i$ and visit $j$, the observed count $y_{ij}$ is modelled as $$ N_i \sim \text{NegBin}(\lambda_i, \alpha), \qquad y_{ij} \mid N_i \sim \text{Binomial}(N_i, p_{ij}), $$ where $\lambda_i$ is the expected abundance, $\alpha$ the overdispersion parameter and $p_{ij}$ the detection probability. We modelled $\log \lambda_i$ as a function of habitat and year, and $\operatorname{logit} p_{ij}$ as a function of night temperature, wind speed, moon illumination and time of emptying. All covariates were standardised to mean 0 and SD 1 before fitting. The models were fitted with `pcount()` from the unmarked package [@fiske2011]. We compared candidate models for detection by AIC, following the steps below. Abundance covariates were kept fixed throughout. 1. Fit the full model with all four detection covariates. 2. Drop each covariate in turn and refit; keep covariates whose removal increases AIC by more than 2. 3. Check the goodness of fit of the selected model with a parametric bootstrap (1000 replicates) of the Pearson $\chi^2$ statistic [@mackenzie2004]. 4. Refit the selected model with `K = 500` to confirm that the upper bound of the abundance integration does not affect the estimates. ```{r fit-models, cache=TRUE} umf <- unmarkedFramePCount( y = as.matrix(select(moths_wide, starts_with("count_"))), siteCovs = select(moths_wide, habitat, year_std), obsCovs = obs_covs ) fm_full <- pcount(~ temp + wind + moon + slot ~ habitat + year_std, data = umf, mixture = "NB", K = 300) fm_best <- pcount(~ temp + moon + slot ~ habitat + year_std, data = umf, mixture = "NB", K = 300) p_hat <- predict(fm_best, type = "det") mean_p <- mean(p_hat$Predicted) p_range <- quantile(p_hat$Predicted, c(0.025, 0.975)) ``` # Results Mean detection probability per visit was `r round(mean_p, 2)` (central 95 % range across nights `r round(p_range[1], 2)`–`r round(p_range[2], 2)`). Detection increased strongly with night temperature and decreased with moon illumination (Figure \@ref(fig:detection)), consistent with earlier studies of light-trap efficiency [@yela1997; @jonason2014]. Wind speed had no detectable effect once temperature was included. ```{r detection, fig.cap="Estimated detection probability as a function of night temperature at new moon (solid line) and full moon (dashed line). Shaded bands are 95 % confidence intervals."} newdat <- expand_grid(temp = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 50), moon = c(-1.2, 1.4), slot = "01:00") predict(fm_best, type = "det", newdata = newdat, appendData = TRUE) |> ggplot(aes(temp, Predicted, linetype = factor(moon, labels = c("New moon", "Full moon")))) + geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper, group = moon), fill = "grey85", colour = NA) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + labs(x = "Night temperature (standardised)", y = "Detection probability", linetype = NULL) + theme_classic() ``` The corrected abundance trend (−2.1 % per year) is weaker than the trend in raw counts (−2.8 % per year). The difference arises because nights in recent years were warmer on average, so a larger share of the moths present was caught. Ignoring detection would therefore have exaggerated the decline by about one third. See the main text for what this implies for national monitoring schemes, e.g. the Rothamsted Insect Survey. ## Sensitivity analyses {#sensitivity} We repeated the analysis (a) excluding 2020, (b) using only the 04:00 emptying, and (c) replacing the negative-binomial mixture by a Poisson mixture. The trend estimates ranged from −1.8 % to −2.4 % per year. None of the alternative analyses changed the qualitative conclusions. # References {-}
# (APPENDIX) Appendix {-} # Software versions {#software} ```{r session-info} sessioninfo::package_info(c("unmarked", "tidyverse", "knitr", "bookdown"), dependencies = FALSE) |> as_tibble() |> select(package, loadedversion, source) |> knitr::kable(col.names = c("Package", "Version", "Source"), caption = "R packages used in this supplement.") ``` # Detection covariates | Covariate | Unit | Source | |-----------|------|--------| | Night temperature | °C | On-site logger; minimum between 21:00 and 04:00 | | Wind speed | m s^-1^ | Nearest DWD weather station | | Moon illumination | fraction | `suncalc::getMoonIllumination()` | | Time of emptying | categorical | 23:00, 01:00 or 04:00 |

171	Our results confirm that flying-insect biomass in protected grasslands has declined substantially over the last two decades, although the decline is less steep than the 76 % reported by @hallmann2017 for a longer period. Because our design held sites, traps and protocols constant, the estimate is unlikely to be an artefact of site turnover, which has been suggested as an explanation for some earlier results [@didham2020]. The stronger decline in wet meadows is consistent with the drying of these habitats during the exceptionally dry summers of 2018, 2019 and 2022, an effect that our season-level weather covariates may not capture fully.
172	
173	Several limitations should be kept in mind. Biomass is a coarse measure that can mask changes in community composition: a decline in large-bodied species may be offset by an increase in small ones, or vice versa. Malaise traps also sample a specific part of the flying-insect community, dominated by Diptera and Hymenoptera, and say little about ground-dwelling or nocturnal taxa. Finally, although all sites are protected, most are small and surrounded by intensively managed farmland, so the trends we observe may reflect pressures acting at the landscape scale rather than within the reserves themselves (see @sec-methods for the site selection criteria).
